reader_question: Where can a city adopt ranked-choice voting, and where has the state ruled it out?
grade_line: Documented: state laws compiled by Ballotpedia, a secondary source, and checked against the atlas
title: Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting as of November 2026, 17 of them in all elections.
measure_line: State laws that prohibit ranked-choice voting, by scope, 50 states and the District of Columbia, as of November 2026. Each square is one state.
notes: Ranked-choice voting: voters rank candidates in order; if no one wins a majority of first choices, the last-place candidate drops out and those ballots count for their next choice, round by round.
Thirty-one states and DC have no state ban. A state with no ban may still keep its cities from adopting it, because many cities need the state’s permission. The map shows bans only.
Twelve of the 19 bans became law in 2024 or 2025. Each square is one state, whatever its size.

Ohio: Bars ranked-choice voting except where Article X or XVIII of the Ohio Constitution permits it; home-rule cities may still adopt it, but lose state local government fund distributions while it is in effect.

Tennessee: Bars county election commissions from using it for a statewide or local government office; federal offices are not named. Signed by the governor February 28, 2022; Public Chapter 621 assigned March 7, 2022, the date Ballotpedia gives as signing.

Ballotpedia reads 17 of the bans as covering all elections; Mississippi’s quoted text does not name congressional races. Ballotpedia is a secondary source. The atlas cites the National Conference of State Legislatures and lists the same 19 states in repair-log entry RL47.
source_line: Source: Ballotpedia, Ranked-choice voting (RCV), state laws prohibiting RCV, as of November 2026, 50 states and DC. Retrieved November 6, 2026. Ohio’s and Tennessee’s bans cover some elections; the other 17 cover all.
alt: A tile map with one square per state. Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting as of November 2026: 17 in all elections, from Florida in 2022 to Indiana in 2026, and Ohio and Tennessee in some elections. The other 31 states and DC have no state ban.
chart_notes: Key: bans it in all elections, with the year it became law; bans it in some elections, Ohio and Tennessee; no state ban, 31 states and DC.
